title: SA public pool standard: scope, definitions and responsibility
audience: Pool and spa service workers, supervisors and operators working on public pools in SA. The South Australian figures apply to public pools under the state standard; applicability to private pools and other states has not yet been confirmed, so check with the relevant regulator before relying on this point.
learningOutcomes: Identify the pool and spa types the South Australian standard covers.
Define owner, operator and knowledgeable person in the standard's terms.
Explain who answers for water quality while bathers are using a public pool.
State where the South Australian figures stop applying and what must be confirmed first.

instruction.heading: What the standard is and what it covers
instruction.body: This South Australian standard, last revised in 2013, sits under the state's 2011 public health legislation. Its scope takes in swimming, spa, waterslide and hydrotherapy facilities, using the wording of the 2013 general regulations. Councils rely on it when enforcing the law, and owners and operators treat it as a practical guide. Some disinfection provisions are adopted by the regulations themselves, so falling short of them carries penalties under those regulations. Because the document is dated, check the current regulation text before you act on any number taken from it.

instruction.heading: Why water quality rules exist
instruction.body: Bathers carry more into a pool than most people expect. Micro-organisms, saliva, sweat, urine, skin cells, hair, sunscreen and dirt all reach the water. Water that is untreated or poorly treated may lead to infections of the eyes, ears, skin and gut. The standard links fatal amoebic meningoencephalitis cases in SA to pools that were neglected, and it notes that unbalanced chemistry can cause rashes and red eyes. Spas and hydrotherapy pools carry more risk, since warm, bubbling water lets microbes multiply fast, and a small spa can host a crowd that is heavy for its volume.

instruction.heading: Definitions you will use on site
instruction.body: A knowledgeable person has the know-how to take charge of public pool operations so its water meets the regulations. An operator runs the pool day to day, understands how it works, and is capable enough to keep it compliant. An owner or occupier is anyone with a right to occupy or direct the premises, including whoever is responsible for them day to day. Free chlorine is the uncombined portion that can still act on organisms. Total chlorine is the free portion plus the combined portion. Turnover rate is the time needed to cycle a volume equal to the entire basin through the filter media. Bather load is the number of people in the water at one time.

instruction.heading: Responsibility for water quality
instruction.body: An owner needs to ensure a capable, knowledgeable person runs a public pool any time users can enter it. Whenever the public can use the pool, owner and operator both answer for keeping the water within the required limits. If an operator lets the water fall out of line, the authority may rule that person unfit for the role and tell the owner to appoint a qualified replacement. Hydrotherapy pools follow the same principle and also expect trained supervision of users who have an impairment.

instruction.heading: Where this standard stops
instruction.body: This is an official South Australian source, and it takes priority over informal, foreign or generic pool advice that conflicts with it. Its figures are aimed at public facilities in SA. Other states and territories have their own rules, and none of them have been checked here. A site operator plan must not conflict with the regulations. Completing this lesson does not give anyone authority to operate a pool.

procedure: Identify the pool type on site: swimming pool, spa, waterslide pool or hydrotherapy pool.
Confirm whether the pool is public, meaning open to members of the public, which places it under the regulations.
Find the named operator or knowledgeable person for the site and record the name.
If the pool is private or in another state, leave the figures out and find the applicable rules before acting on them.
Escalate to the operator any gap between site arrangements and the requirements above.

workedExamples.situation: A council-run leisure centre has a 25 m lap pool and a heated spa. A contractor has been asked to balance the spa water, but no one on site is named as the operator.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Who must be in control of the spa, and what should you do before you touch the chemistry?
workedExamples.reasoning: An owner has to make sure a capable, knowledgeable person is in control whenever members of the public can use the spa. Without a named operator, do not take on responsibility for the water. Record the gap, tell the facility manager, and ask for the operator's name in writing before the spa opens.

equipmentAndPpe: Site record sheet showing pool type, public or private status, state and operator name
Current operator plan or site instructions
Safety glasses and non-slip footwear for any pool-edge inspection

commonErrors.error: Assuming the owner's duty ends once a contractor is hired.
commonErrors.prevention: The owner's duty continues. Confirm who the operator is and that they are competent before work starts.

commonErrors.error: Treating the operator as a job title with no real responsibility.
commonErrors.prevention: The operator controls and manages the pool and must keep it compliant. Check that they do.

commonErrors.error: Applying South Australian figures to every pool without checking.
commonErrors.prevention: Record pool type, public or private status and state first. Leave anything unchecked out.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The disinfection provisions of the standard are adopted by the 2013 regulations. Breaching them is an offence with penalties given in the regulations. Confirm the current regulation text before relying on the numbers.
Drowning and infection risk rises when the operator is not competent. Do not begin work on the water where the operator is unknown.

qualityStandard: Pool type, public or private status and state are recorded before any work starts.
A named operator or knowledgeable person is confirmed in writing for each public pool.
Every figure used in later lessons is traced to a section of the standard or left out.
documentationEvidence: Site record showing pool type, status, jurisdiction and named operator
Note of any gap escalated to the operator, with date and recipient
summary: The standard applies to public swimming, spa, waterslide and hydrotherapy facilities, matching the 2013 regulations' definitions.
An owner has to make sure a capable, knowledgeable person runs the pool, while the operator is accountable for compliance.
The figures are South Australian and dated. Confirm applicability before using them anywhere else.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which term describes a person with enough know-how to take charge of public pool operations so it meets the regulations?
A private pool in SA is being serviced. What is the correct position on the standard's figures?
options: Apply every figure exactly as written, since the standard covers all pool types.
Check applicability to private pools before relying on the figures
Set the standard aside, because it covers only commercial pools in the city
Use the figures from the nearest interstate council

knowledgeChecks.question: The facility is open to bathers. Who shares responsibility for the water?
options: The bathers, who test the water
